title: test: prove Herdr focus-flash Part C fallback without a wrong-focus sample
body:
## Intent The captain chose A: "proceed with a". All 13 upstream PRs in the triage report are approved, opened from Thoughts-One/firstmate-contrib. This PR: Upstream: make the Herdr focus-flash Part C fallback proof non-vacuous. The Part C fallback path in tests/fm-backend-herdr-focus-flash-e2e.test.sh currently requires at least one sampled wrong-focus observation on a defective Herdr release, and fails outright when the wrong-focus window is shorter than one focus-sampling interval, even though the fallback itself ran and restored focus correctly. Prove the fallback ran and restored focus from the plain-close call log and the exact post-close focus instead, without requiring a nonzero wrong-focus sample count. ## What Changed - The Part C defective-release branch in `tests/fm-backend-herdr-focus-flash-e2e.test.sh` no longer fails when the sampler records no wrong-focus sample. It now uses the plain-close call log and the exact post-close focus check as proof that the fallback ran and restored the anchor. It reports the sampler's wrong-focus count in the pass message but does not require that count to be above zero. - `docs/verification/runtime-backends.md` now explains the new Part C proof: the wrong-focus window can be shorter than one focus snapshot. It also states that the 0.7.5 line records the wording of that dated run, and it gives the new pass message. ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: This is a bounded test-only change. It removes the required nonzero wrong-focus sample count and keeps the unconditional checks for plain-close in the call log, exhausted proof, and exact post-close focus. The revert in the fix round follows the user's instructions exactly, and the docs quote the current pass message word for word. ## Testing I ran the real Herdr focus-flash e2e test through bin/fm-herdr-lab.sh in named fm-lab-* sessions, and the default-session tripwire was armed on every run. On 0.9.1, all six checks passed. On a downloaded 0.7.5 release, the changed defective-release branch passed three runs out of three with the new message, and each run recorded 4 wrong-focus observations. I then ran adversarial copies on 0.7.5. With a wrong-focus window shorter than one sample (simulated by the filter), the base test failed with the vacuous "observed no wrong-focus sample" error, and the changed test passed with 0 observations. That shows the flakiness this change targets is fixed. With the restore backstop disabled, the changed test still failed on "left focus off the anchor", so the proof is not vacuous. I deleted all temporary copies and the downloaded binary. The worktree is clean. This change has no UI surface, so the evidence is CLI transcripts only. - Live validation: ✅ go - 5 of 5 scenarios driven live against the product | Scenario | Result | Live | Evidence | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | On a defective release (0.7.5), the Part C fallback passes on the plain-close call log and the exact restored focus, and prints the documented message with the sampler count | ✅ pass | live | focus-flash-e2e-herdr-0.7.5-run1..3.txt: 3/3 exit 0, 'call log proved plain close and final focus was restored to the anchor (sampler wrong-focus observations: 4)' | | Regression: on a defective release, a wrong-focus window shorter than one sampling interval no longer fails the test (the base version fails, the changed version passes) | ✅ pass | live | adversarial-0.7.5-base-miss.txt (base: not ok, vacuous sampler failure) vs adversarial-0.7.5-new-miss.txt (changed: ok, 0 observations) | | Guard: when the restore backstop does not return focus to the anchor, Part C still fails on a defective release | ✅ pass | live | adversarial-0.7.5-new-norestore.txt: 'not ok - the fallback close left focus off the anchor', exit 1 | | On a focus-preserving release (0.9.1), the Part C fallback still requires zero wrong-focus samples and the whole suite passes | ✅ pass | live | focus-flash-e2e-herdr-0.9.1.txt: exit 0, 'fallback on a focus-preserving release: the plain explicit close preserved exact focus throughout' | | The quoted rerun message in docs/verification/runtime-backends.md matches what the test prints on a defective release | ✅ pass | live | The 0.7.5 run output line matches the docs line 1326 text exactly, except for the <count> placeholder |

✅ **intent** - passed ✅ No issues found.
✅ **Rebase** - passed ✅ No issues found.
🔧 **Review** - 1 issue found → auto-fixed (2) ✅ - ⚠️ `tests/fm-backend-herdr-focus-flash-e2e.test.sh:343` - On a defective release, the Part C branch no longer has any evidence that the fallback displaced focus or that the restore backstop ran. The removed `C_WRONG -ge 1` check was the only such evidence, and nothing replaced it. The remaining checks are `pane process-info` exhausted, `pane close` present, and `C_AFTER == C_BEFORE`. The focus-preserving branch applies the same checks, so they would also pass if the plain close never moved focus at all. The pass message says "final focus was restored to the anchor", and the comment says the post-close focus "proves that its restore backstop returned to the anchor". Both overstate what is checked. In the source, `fm_backend_herdr_projection_focus_restore` (bin/backends/herdr.sh:919-948) only calls `fm_backend_herdr_cli ... tab focus` when it sees wrong focus, and the test's `fm_backend_herdr_cli` override writes that call to `C_CALL_LOG`. On 0.7.5 the explicit-close focus change persists until something restores it. Part A shows this at tests/...:118-121, where it has to issue `lab tab focus` itself. So the restore call is always in the call log when STEAL_LIVE=1. Fix: inside the STEAL_LIVE=1 branch, add `grep -q '^tab focus' "$C_CALL_LOG" || fail 'Part C on a defective release never issued the restore backstop tab focus, so no restore was proven'`. This keeps the proof tied to the plain-close call log, as the intent requires, without asking the sampler to catch the brief wrong-focus window. Part B already checks `^tab focus` in the call log (line 200). 🔧 Fix applied. 1 warning still open: - ⚠️ `docs/verification/runtime-backends.md:1326` - The fix round changed the test's pass message but did not update the docs. The docs say that a rerun on a defective release prints `ok - fallback on a defective release: call log proved plain close and final focus was restored to the anchor (sampler wrong-focus observations: <count>)`. The test now prints `fallback on a defective release: call log proved plain close and the restore backstop's tab focus (sampler wrong-focus observations: $C_WRONG)` (tests/fm-backend-herdr-focus-flash-e2e.test.sh:346). Line 1325 describes the proof as "the plain-close call log plus the exact post-close focus" and does not mention the `tab focus` call that the test now requires in that call log. An operator who compares a rerun with the docs gets a string that does not match. Fix: make the quoted line match the test's current pass message, and say on line 1325 that the call log must also contain the restore backstop's `tab focus`. The other option is to change the test message back to the documented text, if that text stays accurate. 🔧 Fix applied. ✅ Re-checked - no issues remain.

the fallback close left focus off the anchor', exit 1 | | On a focus-preserving release (0.9.1), the Part C fallback still requires zero wrong-focus samples and the whole suite passes | ✅ pass | live | focus-flash-e2e-herdr-0.9.1.txt: exit 0, 'fallback on a focus-preserving release: the plain explicit close preserved exact focus throughout' | | The quoted rerun message in docs/verification/runtime-backends.md matches what the test prints on a defective release | ✅ pass | live | The 0.7.5 run output line matches the docs line 1326 text exactly, except for the <count> placeholder | - title: fix(bin): keep watcher lock recovery from stalling the feedback listener
body:
## Intent Fix the automatic Lavish feedback listener so it stays connected without requiring the captain to understand or operate watcher locks, paths, worker IDs, terminal backends, review polling, cleanup commands, or event-record storage. The current failure makes Lavish say the agent is not listening and strands product feedback; this is not workable. Keep those management-system details behind Firstmate. Preserve the captain-facing workflow: open the newest prototype, leave comments, and have those comments reliably reach the responsible worker. ## What Changed - `bin/fm-wake-lib.sh`: A dead `.steal` now gets recovered under one fixed `.steal.recovery` mutex. Before, each retry added another `.steal` suffix, so the nesting had no limit. A recovery mutex is reclaimed only after its holder PID and that PID's process group are proven gone. The reclaim moves the holder record into a quarantine dir in one atomic `mv`. A dangling recovery symlink is cleared, and the acquire tries again. A recovery holder that is still alive, or whose process group is still alive, is waited out. `fm_lock_remove_stray_owner_link` now pairs `.steal` locks with `.recovery` and never recurses past `.steal.recovery`. - `fm_lock_try_acquire` now returns `2` when the recovery mutex cannot be reclaimed. That happens when the holder cannot be proven gone or the mutex directory cannot be written. The new `fm_lock_acquire_wait_refusable` passes that `2` back to the caller. So do `fm_lock_acquire_wait_bounded` and the wait-handoff helper. `fm_lock_acquire_wait` keeps its old never-fail contract. It prints the refusal once, then keeps waiting. `fm_procevent_source_lock_acquire` in `bin/fm-procevent-lib.sh` now uses the refusable wait. - `tests/fm-watcher-lock.test.sh` and `tests/fm-procevent.test.sh` get new tests for bounded steal recovery. They cover reclaiming a dead recovery mutex, clearing dangling recovery links, waiting out live holders and process groups, and the procevent source lock returning a refusal instead of hanging. ## Risk Assessment ⚠️ Medium: The latest fix is narrow and correct: a live recovery-holder process group now returns 1 (retry) instead of 2 (refusal), so the Lavish listener waits and then resumes without touching owner evidence. The branch still reworks a shared, concurrency-sensitive lock primitive that many callers use, so it deserves normal caution. ## Testing I ran the two test files that hold the new lock tests: fm-watcher-lock and fm-procevent. Every new test passed: recovering a dead recovery holder, refusing a live one, waiting through a live process group, handling a leftover legacy .steal.steal, handling a self-held lock, and handling a dangling recovery link. The Lavish arm tests also passed: bounded refusal, and waiting through a live group, then resuming. One older retry-listener check in fm-procevent failed once, after a 10-second wait, while the machine load was about 19. It passed on a rerun of the same target code, and it passes on the base commit, so it is a timing flake and not a product bug. A manual Lavish arm run with four dead leftover locks reconnected the listener in under a second, with no new nested lock paths. This is CLI-only work, so there is no visual surface to screenshot.
Evidence: End-to-end Lavish arm with leftover dead locks (new code) Source: [End-to-end Lavish arm with leftover dead locks (new code)](https://github.com/prishsu0730/firstmate/blob/67e2f4ad884aeea1e2f5ffe2d330ac60cc3bc1b2/.no-mistakes/evidence/fm/fm-lavish-listener-lock/demo-lavish-arm-new.txt) == before: <src>.lock, .lock.steal, .lock.steal.recovery, .lock.steal.steal (all dead pid) RESULT: arm exit=0 after 0s registered: <src> (lavish) armed: <src> == after: only the inert legacy <src>.lock.steal.steal remains; registration present ```text ##### NEW CODE (target 85f14f4) == before: leftover lock dirs (all owned by dead pid 99999999) .lock .lock.steal .lock.steal.recovery .lock.steal.steal == run: fm-procevent-lavish.sh arm board.html (20s cap) RESULT: arm exit=0 after 0s stdout: registered: (lavish) armed: artifact: /private/tmp/fm-demo.sTca/board.html stderr: == after: lock dirs .lock.steal.steal == registration still present: yes ```
Evidence: Same demo on base code (comparison) Source: [Same demo on base code (comparison)](https://github.com/prishsu0730/firstmate/blob/67e2f4ad884aeea1e2f5ffe2d330ac60cc3bc1b2/.no-mistakes/evidence/fm/fm-lavish-listener-lock/demo-lavish-arm-base.txt) ```text ##### OLD CODE (base 9296f9b) == before: leftover lock dirs (all owned by dead pid 99999999) .lock .lock.steal .lock.steal.recovery .lock.steal.steal == run: fm-procevent-lavish.sh arm board.html (20s cap) RESULT: arm exit=0 after 1s stdout: registered: (lavish) armed: artifact: /private/tmp/fm-demo.KeYV/board.html stderr: == after: lock dirs .lock.steal.recovery == registration still present: yes ```
Evidence: Demo script Source: [Demo script](https://github.com/prishsu0730/firstmate/blob/67e2f4ad884aeea1e2f5ffe2d330ac60cc3bc1b2/.no-mistakes/evidence/fm/fm-lavish-listener-lock/demo-lavish-arm-with-wedged-locks.sh) ```text #!/usr/bin/env bash # Demo: Lavish arm with leftover broken lock state a real home can hold. # Usage: demo.sh set -u ROOT=$1; T=$(mktemp -d /tmp/fm-demo.XXXX) mkdir -p "$T/home/state" "$T/claims" "$T/bin" printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\nexit 0\n' > "$T/bin/lavish-axi"; chmod +x "$T/bin/lavish-axi" printf '

newest prototype

\n' > "$T/board.html" run() { PATH="$T/bin:$PATH" FM_HOME="$T/home" FM_PROCEVENT_CLAIM_ROOT="$T/claims" "$ROOT/bin/fm-procevent-lavish.sh" "$@"; } id=$(run source-id "$T/board.html") run arm "$T/board.html" >/dev/null || { echo "seed arm failed"; exit 1; } dead=99999999; while kill -0 $dead 2>/dev/null; do dead=$((dead+1)); done L="$T/claims/$id.lock" for d in "$L" "$L.steal" "$L.steal.steal" "$L.steal.recovery"; do mkdir -p "$d"; echo $dead > "$d/pid"; done echo "== before: leftover lock dirs (all owned by dead pid $dead)"; (cd "$T/claims" && ls -d *.lock* | sed "s/$id//") echo "== run: fm-procevent-lavish.sh arm board.html (20s cap)" start=$SECONDS PATH="$T/bin:$PATH" FM_HOME="$T/home" FM_PROCEVENT_CLAIM_ROOT="$T/claims" "$ROOT/bin/fm-procevent-lavish.sh" arm "$T/board.html" >"$T/out" 2>"$T/err" & p=$! while kill -0 $p 2>/dev/null && [ $((SECONDS-start)) -lt 20 ]; do sleep 0.2; done if kill -0 $p 2>/dev/null; then kill -TERM $p; wait $p 2>/dev/null; echo "RESULT: arm HUNG past 20s (listener cannot reconnect)" else wait $p; echo "RESULT: arm exit=$? after $((SECONDS-start))s"; fi echo "stdout:"; sed "s/$id//g" "$T/out" | head -5; echo "stderr:"; sed "s/$id//g" "$T/err" | head -5 echo "== after: lock dirs"; (cd "$T/claims" && ls -d *.lock* 2>/dev/null | sed "s/$id//" || echo "(none)") echo "== registration still present:"; ls "$T/home/state/procevent/$id.source" >/dev/null && echo yes PATH="$T/bin:$PATH" FM_HOME="$T/home" "$ROOT/bin/fm-procevent.sh" retire "$id" >/dev/null 2>&1 trash "$T" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$T" ```
Evidence: fm-watcher-lock test log (new recovery tests) Source: [fm-watcher-lock test log (new recovery tests)](https://github.com/prishsu0730/firstmate/blob/67e2f4ad884aeea1e2f5ffe2d330ac60cc3bc1b2/.no-mistakes/evidence/fm/fm-lavish-listener-lock/fm-watcher-lock.test.log) ```text ok - wait deadline diagnoses and reaps a stopped test child without hanging ok - simultaneous watcher starts leave exactly one live process ok - fm_pid_identity real ps fallback is locale-invariant ok - fm_pid_identity is locale-invariant across LC_ALL/LC_TIME ok - /proc process identity ignores simulated btime changes ok - /proc process identity detects pid reuse ok - MSYS /proc process identity regression skipped on non-Windows host ok - killed watcher stale lock is reclaimed tests/fm-watcher-lock.test.sh: line 1294: 31473 Killed: 9 FM_STATE_OVERRIDE="$state" bash -c ' . "$1" fm_lock_remove_path() { if [ "$1" = "$STATE/.watch.lock" ]; then kill -KILL "${BASHPID:-$$}" fi return 1 } fm_lock_try_acquire "$2" ' _ "$LIB" "$lockdir" > /dev/null 2>&1 ok - stale watcher reclaim publishes durable recovery evidence before clear ok - live watcher lock with stale heartbeat is actionable ok - guard banner leads when down with pending wakes (repair-after-drain) and stays silent when live and fresh ok - concurrent fm_lock_try_acquire yields exactly one winner ok - dead-pid stale lock is reclaimed by a single acquirer ok - concurrent stale-lock steal yields exactly one winner ok - live steal mutex is not reclaimed ok - dead recovery-mutex holder is reclaimed without a nested mutex ok - live recovery-mutex holder is not reclaimed ok - recovery mutex with a live process group is waited out, then recovered once it exits ok - legacy nested steal leftover does not wedge the lock ok - self-held steal and recovery mutexes are reclaimed by their own process ok - dangling recovery link is cleared and retried instead of refused ok - live-held lock is not stolen ok - empty mid-acquire lock keeps a minimum grace ok - late original claimant cannot claim a recreated lock ok - paused mid-acquire claimant backs off to active stealer ok - watch restart preserves recovery without signaling a reused pid ok - watch restart attaches to a verified healthy peer and later surfaces a successor gap ok - It returns 2 whenever `fm_lock_reclaim_dead_recovery` cannot prove absence. One case: the dead recovery holder was a process-group leader, and a child of it still runs (for example a `sleep` or `lavish-axi poll` left behind after SIGKILL). `kill -0 -pid` then succeeds, so every acquire refuses. The callers at `bin/fm-procevent.sh:511`, `:551`, `:942`, `:1873` and `:1944` run `die "cannot lock the source"`. So the listener exits until that orphaned child ends, and nothing reclaims the mutex once it does. The intent says the listener must "stay connected without requiring the captain to understand or operate watcher locks". The group-absence proof was a user requirement. But the choice to hard-fail the listener, instead of waiting it out quietly like `fm_lock_acquire_wait`, is a product call. Two processes can then both believe they hold the recovery mutex. The later `.steal` recheck and the primary recheck narrow the damage, but the window exists. A durable version would rename the link to a unique quarantine name, verify it, and then discard it or put it back, which is the same pattern already used for the holder directory. The window is tiny, so this is not blocking. - ℹ️ `bin/fm-wake-lib.sh:520` - The recovery mutex for a `.steal` lock moved from `.steal.steal` to `.steal.recovery`, and claims on `.steal` are no longer blocked by `.steal.steal`. During an upgrade, one old and one new process can recover the same dead `.steal` under different mutexes, so they are not serialized against each other. The later recheck against the primary lock limits the effect. Restarting the listeners after the upgrade closes the gap. 🔧 Fix: Wait out live recovery-holder process groups instead of refusing ✅ Re-checked - no issues remain.

title: test: match the --serve child by command line in orphan-reap test
body:
## Intent

The captain chose to proceed with submitting the upstream contribution PRs identified by triaging the private firstmate fork against current upstream main, opened from the Thoughts-One/firstmate-contrib public fork. This PR fixes a process-selection race in tests/fm-remote-job-orphan-reap.test.sh: the test identifies the fixture worker's real long-lived --serve child by taking pgrep's first result under the worker's pid immediately after any child appears. The worker's own Linux start path runs several short-lived setup children (platform detection, home and root canonicalization, state preparation) before it forks the long-lived --serve process, so that first-child pgrep can catch one of those setup children instead of the real serving process, and by the next line find it already exited, making the test flaky. Fix it by identifying the serving child through its exact --serve command line instead of taking the first child that appears.

## What Changed
- Adds a `wait_serve` helper to `tests/fm-remote-job-orphan-reap.test.sh`. The helper polls `pgrep -f` for the exact `/bin/bash <root>/bin/fm-remote-job-worker.sh --serve` command line and returns that pid. Before, the test used the first child that `pgrep -P` found under the worker, and that child could be a short-lived setup subprocess.
- Replaces the `wait_child` + `pgrep -P ... | head -n 1` lookups with `wait_serve` for the first serving child (`SERVE`) and for the respawned child (`SURVIVOR`). The respawn wait now happens where `SURVIVOR` is captured and keeps its 15-second timeout and failure message.

## Risk Assessment

✅ Low: This is a test-only change. It replaces the first-child pgrep with an exact match on the `--serve` command line, using the same anchored pattern that start_worker() already uses. The worker's supervisor has transient children (command substitutions for platform detection, canonicalization, prepare_state, and cleanup, plus the backoff `sleep`), and none of them has that command line. The `--serve` process's own subshells do match, but they always have higher pids than `--serve` and `head -n 1` picks the lowest. The fix-round change moves the respawn wait into the SURVIVOR assignment exactly as the user instructed, and the test's assertions otherwise stay the same.

## Testing

I ran the changed test 8 times. I also ran three probe scripts against the real fixture worker, which the test starts through the library's Linux start path. The probes compare the old first-child selector with the new `--serve` command-line selector. The new selector returned the real `--serve` process in every trial. In the respawn window, the old selector returned a short-lived `sleep 1` in 6 of 6 trials. That result proves the defect and the fix. On this host, the setup children at first spawn finished too quickly to observe, so I could not reproduce that part of the race live. Case 1 passed in all 8 runs. Case 2 is unchanged and failed in 2 of 8 runs because a machine-wide reaper from another concurrent no-mistakes run stopped its stand-in worker. This change has no UI, so there are no screenshots. The evidence is the CLI transcripts.

- Live validation: ✅ go - 2 of 3 scenarios driven live against the product

| Scenario | Result | Live | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The test identifies the real --serve child of a freshly started worker and case 1 passes | ✅ pass | live | after-fix-5-runs.log, after-fix-runs-6-8.log: all 8 runs print 'ok' for the process-group, orphan, never-reaped, and prune cases; probe-first-child-race.log: wait_serve returned the `--serve` pid in 1… |
| Adversarial: after the --serve child is killed, the test selects the respawned --serve process and not the transient backoff/setup child | ✅ pass | live | probe-respawn-child.log: the old selector returned `sleep 1` (exited moments later) in 6 of 6 trials; wait_serve returned `/bin/bash .../fm-remote-job-worker.sh --serve` in 6 of 6 |
| Adversarial: at initial spawn, a short-lived setup child appears before --serve and the old first-child selector picks it | ⏸️ untested | no | On this fast host, the setup command substitutions ended before pgrep could see them, so I could not reproduce the initial-spawn window live. The new selector is still correct, because it matches only… |

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# After killing the real --serve child, compare the OLD selector (wait_child + first pgrep -P child)
# with the NEW wait_serve selector for identifying the respawned serving child.
set -u
W=$1; N=${2:-6}
T=$(mktemp -d /tmp/fm-probe.XXXXXX); T=$(cd $T && pwd -P)
for i in $(seq 1 $N); do
  r=$T/r$i; mkdir -p $r/bin $T/a$i
  cp $W/bin/fm-remote-job-lib.sh $W/bin/fm-remote-job-worker.sh $r/bin/; chmod +x $r/bin/*.sh
  echo f > $r/AGENTS.md; git -C $r init -qb main; git -C $r -c user.email=t@e -c user.name=t add -A; git -C $r -c user.email=t@e -c user.name=t commit -qm x
  ( export FM_REMOTE_JOB_STATE_ROOT=$T/s$i FM_REMOTE_JOB_PLATFORM_OVERRIDE=Linux
    . $W/bin/fm-remote-job-lib.sh; fm_remote_job_start_linux_worker $r $T/a$i >/dev/null 2>&1 )
  wk=""; for _ in $(seq 100); do wk=$(pgrep -f "^/bin/bash $r/bin/fm-remote-job-worker.sh\$"|head -n1); [ -n "$wk" ] && break; sleep 0.02; done
  sv=""; for _ in $(seq 100); do sv=$(pgrep -f "^/bin/bash $r/bin/fm-remote-job-worker.sh --serve\$"|head -n1); [ -n "$sv" ] && break; sleep 0.1; done
  kill -KILL $sv; while kill -0 $sv 2>/dev/null; do sleep 0.05; done
  for _ in $(seq 500); do [ -n "$(pgrep -P $wk)" ] && break; sleep 0.01; done
  old=$(pgrep -P $wk | head -n1); oldcmd=$(ps -o args= -p "$old" 2>/dev/null)
  new=""; for _ in $(seq 150); do new=$(pgrep -f "^/bin/bash $r/bin/fm-remote-job-worker.sh --serve\$"|head -n1); [ -n "$new" ] && break; sleep 0.1; done
  newcmd=$(ps -o args= -p "$new" 2>/dev/null)
  kill -0 "$old" 2>/dev/null && oa=alive || oa=GONE
  printf 'respawn %d | killed serve=%s\n  OLD first-child pid=%s cmd=[%s] alive-later=%s\n  NEW wait_serve  pid=%s cmd=[%s]\n' $i $sv "$old" "${oldcmd:-<exited>}" $oa "$new" "$newcmd"
  kill -KILL -- -$wk 2>/dev/null; kill -KILL $wk 2>/dev/null
done
rm -rf $T

title: fix(bin): recover missing tmux worker endpoints safely
body:
## Intent

Find and implement a safe solution when a Car Remodel worker restart is refused because its recorded terminal no longer exists. Preserve the existing work and restart the worker so validation can continue.

## What Changed

- Added `fm_backend_tmux_bound_session` (`bin/backends/tmux.sh`) to verify the calling process's `TMUX`/`TMUX_PANE` against the live tmux server (pid, pane id, session name) before trusting any session identity derived from ambient state.
- Taught `fm_control_endpoint_absence_verdict` (`bin/fm-control-lib.sh`) to prove tmux endpoint absence: it now requires a verified seat bound to the recorded session, then classifies the target as `gone`, `dead`, or `alive` instead of always returning `unproven` for tmux.
- Wired the new absence proof into `bin/fm-control.sh` (`exit`/`relaunch`) and `bin/fm-spawn.sh` (relaunch recovery path) so a tmux `missing` endpoint proven gone can now recreate the exact recorded session/window and rebind the task, with matching abort-cleanup handling (`TMUX_RECREATE_ABORT_CLEANUP`/`TMUX_RECREATE_ABORT_TARGET`) to remove an unused recreated endpoint if the relaunch aborts; unbound, cross-session, or unproven tmux requests still refuse.
- Updated `docs/agent-control.md`, `docs/tmux-backend.md`, `docs/verification/runtime-backends.md`, and `.agents/skills/stuck-crewmate-recovery/SKILL.md` to describe the new tmux recovery behavior in place of the prior always-refuse documentation, and extended `tests/fm-backend-tmux-smoke.test.sh` and `tests/fm-control-relaunch.test.sh` with coverage for the recreate/rebind and abort-cleanup paths.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Risk Assessment

✅ Low: The change adds a well-bounded, cryptographically-sound-in-spirit seat-verification (server PID + pane identity check against the live tmux server) that closes a previously acknowledged gap, is guarded by existing locking, has matching abort/rollback cleanup wired through the established pattern, and is backed by both a real-tmux integration test and a stubbed transactional test (including a dedicated Car Remodel preservation scenario) that assert observable state rather than source content.

## Testing

Only one scenario was driven live (real tmux server, real bin/backends/tmux.sh + bin/fm-control-lib.sh). The Car Remodel preserve-and-restart scenario and its adversarial refusal/rollback/concurrency guards were run through the CLI-level fm-spawn/fm-control relaunch suite against a scripted tmux double rather than a real tmux server, so per the live-validation contract those six scenarios are corrected from "pass" to "untested" here. Suite execution stopped later on an unrelated, pre-existing tasks-axi version gap (0.2.5 installed vs 0.2.6+ required) in a backlog-transition idempotency test this diff does not touch.

title: test: fake-clock the remote-job queue and execution-window test
body:
## Intent All 13 upstream PRs in the triage report are approved, opened from Thoughts-One/firstmate-contrib. This PR: Upstream: fake-clock the remote-job queue and execution-window test. Rewrite the "queued jobs receive a fresh bounded execution window" test in tests/fm-remote-job.test.sh to use a fake clock instead of racing real sleeps. The test currently stages two real 1.8s-sleeping jobs against a 5s queue timeout and a 3s execution timeout, racing real sleeps against those bounds, which is a pre-emptive flake under load. The property under test - a queued job's execution deadline is computed fresh at dequeue, not debited by how long it waited - does not need real elapsed time to hold, only a controllable clock. Install a fake date binary on PATH for this file, following the same fake-date-on-PATH convention tests/fm-contributions.test.sh already uses for the same purpose. Block the first job on a marker file instead of sleeping, stage the second job, advance the fake clock to simulate most of the queue wait, then release the first job so the second job dequeues at the advanced time. This is a test-only, general flakiness fix with no fleet-specific content, and it currently reproduces and applies cleanly against upstream's current main. ## What Changed - Adds a fake `date` binary to `PATH` in `tests/fm-remote-job.test.sh`, following the convention in `tests/fm-contributions.test.sh`. `date +%s` returns the value in `FM_REMOTE_JOB_TEST_CLOCK` only while that file exists. In all other cases, the fake binary calls the real `/bin/date`, so the other tests in the file keep the real clock. - Changes the "queued jobs receive a fresh bounded execution window" test so that it no longer uses two real 1.8s sleeping jobs. The first job is a new `fm-block-job.sh`, which waits until a marker file exists. The second job is `fm-touch-job.sh`, which stages behind it. The test moves the fake clock forward 4s, just under the 5s queue timeout, and then creates the marker to release the first job. The second job then dequeues at the advanced time. - The test still checks that the second job exits 0 and writes its side effect within the 3s execution timeout, so it still proves the execution deadline is computed at dequeue. The test deletes the clock file after both jobs finish. ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: The change only touches a test and matches the stated intent. The worker that serves this test inherits the fake date through ensure_worker's `nohup env`. An implementation that takes queue wait out of the execution window gives remaining=0 at the advanced clock, so the test would fail on that bug. The only issues are an unbounded wait if the worker fails and an inaccurate comment. ## Testing I ran the changed test file as written, and the rewritten execution-window test passed. I then mutated the worker so it computes the execution deadline from enqueue time on the fake clock, which is the regression the test must guard. The target test failed at its own assertion. This proves that the fake clock reaches the long-lived worker and that the test still holds the property. Under 2x CPU oversubscription the target test passed again. A different, untouched test in the same file (worker crash recovery) failed under that load; that is recorded as an informational note. The change is test-only and has no user-facing surface beyond the test harness, so the evidence is the test transcripts. The worktree is clean. - Live validation: ✅ go - 3 of 3 scenarios driven live against the product | Scenario | Result | Live | Evidence | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Run the remote-job test file: the queued job gets a fresh execution window after a simulated 4s queue wait and passes | ✅ pass | live | fixed-run.log: `ok - queued jobs receive a fresh bounded execution window`, rc=0 | | Adversarial: the worker debits queue wait from the execution window, and the rewritten test fails | ✅ pass | live | mutation-debit-queue-wait.log: `not ok - queue time consumed the second job's execution timeout` | | Flake resistance: the target test still passes under heavy CPU load | ✅ pass | live | fixed-run-under-load.log: target test ok with 32 CPU hogs on 16 cores |
Evidence: Fixed test run (target test ok) Source: [Fixed test run (target test ok)](https://github.com/Thoughts-One/firstmate-contrib/blob/29ead1ca434da8fada76b665adb61591a648bfca/.no-mistakes/evidence/fm/up-remote-job-fake-clock/fixed-run.log) ```text ok - default queue and execution bounds independently cover long polls ok - operator PATH excludes a symlinked local bin ok - operator PATH honors nvm defaults with a deterministic fallback ok - operator PATH resolves the authorized Nix profile bin link ok - operator PATH orders discovered tool installs deterministically ok - the worker preserves bounded argv and stdin in an empty environment ok - active jobs keep the worker ready for concurrent requests ok - ensure replaces a live worker after its code changes ok - worker identity binds the canonical configured code root ok - stale ownership is reclaimed without signaling a reused pid ok - the worker enforces the job timeout and publishes its result ok - the worker expires queued jobs before they can mutate ok - queued jobs receive a fresh bounded execution window ok - a queued short command preempts a running long poll instead of waiting its window ok - a poll re-armed after preemption reads the same cursor with nothing lost ok - sibling polls never preempt each other into a re-arm churn loop ok - worker shutdown terminates the active command tree before replacement ok - Linux supervision recovers crashes and stops orphaned commands ok - pre-execution validation obeys the job timeout ok - the worker drains bounded output without changing command results ok - the worker refuses symlinked job fields before command execution ok - failed shutdown quarantines ownership against replacement workers ok - quarantine recovery refuses unverifiable supervisors and ignores reused pids ok - a repeatedly signalled shutdown still releases ownership for the next worker ok - barely healthy worker failures remain bounded by the restart guard ALL TESTS PASSED real 1m17.924s user 0m14.681s sys 0m44.380s ```
Evidence: Mutation (queue wait debited) caught by rewritten test Source: [Mutation (queue wait debited) caught by rewritten test](https://github.com/Thoughts-One/firstmate-contrib/blob/29ead1ca434da8fada76b665adb61591a648bfca/.no-mistakes/evidence/fm/up-remote-job-fake-clock/mutation-debit-queue-wait.log) ok - the worker expires queued jobs before they can mutate not ok - queue time consumed the second job's execution timeout ```text ok - default queue and execution bounds independently cover long polls ok - operator PATH excludes a symlinked local bin ok - operator PATH honors nvm defaults with a deterministic fallback ok - operator PATH resolves the authorized Nix profile bin link ok - operator PATH orders discovered tool installs deterministically ok - the worker preserves bounded argv and stdin in an empty environment ok - active jobs keep the worker ready for concurrent requests ok - ensure replaces a live worker after its code changes ok - worker identity binds the canonical configured code root ok - stale ownership is reclaimed without signaling a reused pid ok - the worker enforces the job timeout and publishes its result ok - the worker expires queued jobs before they can mutate not ok - queue time consumed the second job's execution timeout ```
Evidence: Run under 2x CPU oversubscription Source: [Run under 2x CPU oversubscription](https://github.com/Thoughts-One/firstmate-contrib/blob/29ead1ca434da8fada76b665adb61591a648bfca/.no-mistakes/evidence/fm/up-remote-job-fake-clock/fixed-run-under-load.log) ```text ok - default queue and execution bounds independently cover long polls ok - operator PATH excludes a symlinked local bin ok - operator PATH honors nvm defaults with a deterministic fallback ok - operator PATH resolves the authorized Nix profile bin link ok - operator PATH orders discovered tool installs deterministically ok - the worker preserves bounded argv and stdin in an empty environment ok - active jobs keep the worker ready for concurrent requests ok - ensure replaces a live worker after its code changes ok - worker identity binds the canonical configured code root ok - stale ownership is reclaimed without signaling a reused pid ok - the worker enforces the job timeout and publishes its result ok - the worker expires queued jobs before they can mutate ok - queued jobs receive a fresh bounded execution window ok - a queued short command preempts a running long poll instead of waiting its window ok - a poll re-armed after preemption reads the same cursor with nothing lost ok - sibling polls never preempt each other into a re-arm churn loop ok - worker shutdown terminates the active command tree before replacement not ok - worker crash recovery did not publish unknown completion real 2m39.413s user 0m10.066s sys 0m29.457s ```
- Outcome: ⚠️ 1 info across 1 run (6m19s) ## Pipeline Updates from [git push no-mistakes](https://github.com/kunchenguid/no-mistakes)
✅ **intent** - passed ✅ No issues found.
✅ **Rebase** - passed ✅ No issues found.
⚠️ **Review** - 2 infos - ℹ️ `tests/fm-remote-job.test.sh:393` - The fake clock stays frozen at T0+4 while the test runs both `fm_remote_job_wait` calls. It is removed only after they return (line 395). `fm_remote_job_wait` stops at `wait_deadline = queue_deadline + execution_timeout + FM_REMOTE_JOB_WAIT_GRACE` (bin/fm-remote-job-lib.sh:698,723-724), which here is at least T0+8. The frozen `date +%s` keeps returning T0+4, so the wait can never reach that deadline. If the worker dies or never publishes a result, this test hangs until the 30-minute CI job timeout. Before this change, it failed after about 8 seconds with 'remote job did not complete within its bounded wait'. Only the failure path changes, because the worker's own execution bound uses bash `SECONDS` and still ends a normal run. Fix: keep the clock frozen only until the property is captured. After releasing the first job, poll for the second job's `deadline` file with a bounded real-time loop, remove the clock file, and then run the two waits. - ℹ️ `tests/fm-remote-job.test.sh:91` - The new comment says 'The worker started below is long-lived for this whole file, so the fake binary must be on PATH before its first start', and that the clock variable 'stays unset for every other test in this file'. Neither statement matches the code. The worker launched directly at about line 212 gets an explicit `PATH="$RUNTIME_BIN:/usr/bin:/bin:..."` that leaves out fakebin. That worker is replaced several times through `fm_remote_job_ensure_worker`. The test relies on the replacement worker from `nohup env ...` (bin/fm-remote-job-lib.sh:1174), which inherits the exported PATH. Also, `FM_REMOTE_JOB_TEST_CLOCK` is exported for the whole file, and only the file it names is absent outside this test. Update the comment: the worker that ensure_worker restarts inherits the exported PATH and clock variable, and the fake date falls through to the real one until the clock file exists.
⚠️ **Test** - 1 info - ℹ️ `tests/fm-remote-job.test.sh` - Under 2x CPU oversubscription, the unchanged test 'worker crash recovery did not publish unknown completion' in the same file failed. This change does not touch that test, and the fake date falls through to the real date once the clock file is removed. It looks like a separate load-sensitive test that may deserve its own follow-up. - Live validation: ✅ go - 3 of 3 scenarios driven live against the product | Scenario | Result | Live | Evidence | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Run the remote-job test file: the queued job gets a fresh execution window after a simulated 4s queue wait and passes | ✅ pass | live | fixed-run.log: `ok - queued jobs receive a fresh bounded execution window`, rc=0 | | Adversarial: the worker debits queue wait from the execution window, and the rewritten test fails | ✅ pass | live | mutation-debit-queue-wait.log: `not ok - queue time consumed the second job's execution timeout` | | Flake resistance: the target test still passes under heavy CPU load | ✅ pass | live | fixed-run-under-load.log: target test ok with 32 CPU hogs on 16 cores | - `bash tests/fm-remote-job.test.sh` on the change (whole file, which contains the rewritten test): rc=0, target test ok in about 78s - Mutation: set bin/fm-remote-job-worker.sh:889 to `deadline=$(( queue_deadline - FM_REMOTE_JOB_QUEUE_TIMEOUT + timeout + 1 ))` (execution deadline counted from enqueue on the fake clock), then ran `bash tests/fm-remote-job.test.sh`. Result: `not ok - queue time consumed the second job's execution timeout`. Reverted with `git checkout` - `Discarded mutation: a first attempt based on the job-file mtime let real seconds leak in, so it was not a faithful debit. It was replaced by the enqueue-time mutation above` - `bash tests/fm-remote-job.test.sh` with 32 `yes` CPU hogs on 16 cores: target test ok under 2x CPU oversubscription

title: feat(bin): publish and watch Gerrit changes on forge-bound projects
body:
## Intent

Begin the work on the feature branch for firstmate Gerrit integration. If the design doc needs any changes for gerrit-axi, do that first, then handle the delivery mode and monitoring. One was going to be migrated/cherry-picked and the other reimplemented. The eventual goal is to get this feature branch to a PR by end of day.

Context the ask refers to. The plan settled on 2026-09-22: the Gerrit design document (docs/gerrit-forge-integration.md) is the FIRST commit on a feature branch asserting the design, later commits implement it, and ONE pull request carries design and implementation together for a single up-or-down decision. The design commit exists as e9fca859 on local branch fm/fm-gerrit-forge-doc. The design was written while gerrit-axi was read-only (v0.1) and states what the tool "must become": publish and submit powers, never voting. gerrit-axi 0.2.0 has since been released and installed (gerrit-axi --version prints 0.2.0): publish --stack --topic, publish --squash, and submit, with voting structurally impossible.

Two earlier branches hold the implementation material. The monitoring work (record and watch a Gerrit change with the existing provider-tagged PR identity) is forge-neutral and survives the redesign intact, so it migrates. The delivery-mode work encodes the two forge rules the design inverts - it permits local-only forge=gerrit as an inert annotation and refuses direct-PR forge=gerrit, while the design refuses the first and permits the second - so it is reimplemented against the design rather than migrated. Fleet sync for local-only projects stays a separate task and is not part of this branch.

Settled decisions the implementation must honour: the forge is detected and proposed at project intake, with a per-project record as the confirmation; stack-versus-squash mechanics live in the forge tool; the tool gains publish and submit but no voting; a stack is watched by pinned membership, with growth reported rather than absorbed; firstmate never submits or votes on its own authority. The first real-world test will be on SlnkFindMy, a low-stakes Gerrit-hosted project at ~/Code/SlnkFindMy.

On the stack-scope and publisher questions raised mid-task: "yes, A and worker publishing" - option A is that this branch publishes squashed single changes only and refuses shape=stack with the reason, with the pinned-membership stack watch filed as follow-up work; worker publishing means the task worker publishes through gerrit-axi after the pipeline passes, and the one design sentence saying Firstmate pushes is amended to match.

## What Changed

- Adds the Gerrit forge design (`docs/gerrit-forge-integration.md`, `docs/gerrit-change-watch.md`) and a per-project `forge=gerrit` registry binding. `fm-project-mode.sh` now prints `<mode> <yolo> <forge>` and fails closed with exit 3 on an unknown forge, an unrecognized or unterminated annotation token, or `forge=gerrit` on `local-only`. It also forces yolo off for Gerrit projects. The new `bin/fm-forge-detect.sh` suggests the binding at intake from the origin remote's SSH port 29418 or a `refs/for/` push refspec. It never writes the registry.
- Worker briefs on forge-bound `no-mistakes` and `direct-PR` projects (`fm-dod-lib.sh`, `fm-brief.sh`, `fm-spawn.sh`, `fm-promote.sh`) get a `forge=gerrit shape=squash` contract. Under it the worker publishes one squashed change with `gerrit-axi publish --squash` and reports `done: PR <change url> published for review`. The brief forbids `--stack`, `git push`, submitting, voting and abandoning. A Gerrit done is accepted only when the change's current patch set carries the worktree HEAD tree, or when it matches the PR already recorded for the task.
- `fm-pr-lib.sh`, `fm-pr-poll.sh`, `fm-pr-check.sh` and `fm-pr-merge.sh` record and watch a Gerrit change through the existing provider-tagged PR identity, including self-hosted and nested project paths. Fleet sync, home seeding, crew state and review-diff are updated to handle the new forge field. The branch also adds tests for detection, registry parsing, brief rendering and the Gerrit done gate, and updates the matching docs (`AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `docs/`).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Risk Assessment

✅ Low: The fix round does what round 1 asked for. For a done naming a Gerrit URL, the remote-tracking reachability test is now replaced rather than run first. A recorded pr= is accepted without a network read, which keeps a server-side rebase from flipping an armed task back. A live patch-set tree check stays as the gate before arming. The gerrit-axi read is folded into one exact-record helper with the same behaviour, and the new tests would fail if the gate or the record shortcut were removed.

## Testing

I drove the Gerrit forge path end to end against the real Gerrit server and a local clone of SlnkFindMy, using only read-only server calls. Intake detection proposes forge=gerrit from SSH port 29418 or a refs/for/ push refspec, and forge=none for GitHub. The registry binds forge=gerrit on no-mistakes and direct-PR. It refuses local-only+gerrit, mistyped tokens and a bare forge in the mode slot (exit 3), and reports +yolo as off with the stated reason. Briefs render the one-change `gerrit-axi publish --squash` contract, and the no-mistakes one adds `--skip push,pr,ci` and custody recovery. Rule 1 forbids submit, voting and abandoning, and --shape stack is refused. The done gate accepts only when the change's current patch set carries HEAD's tree, and a squash counts because only the tree is compared. It refuses a post-publish commit even when that commit is reachable from a no-mistakes gate ref (the bypass fixed in review). After `fm-pr-check.sh` records pr=, a diverged copy is still accepted and `gerrit-axi` is never called. The poll prints `merged` only for the merged change, stays silent for open and abandoned ones, and works from the armed sidecar outside any repository. Not run live: spawn forge agreement, which is refused inside the no-mistakes gate by design, and a real worker publishing to Gerrit, which is outward-facing. Scratch directories under /tmp were removed and the worktree is clean.

- Live validation: ✅ go - 10 of 12 scenarios driven live against the product

| At intake, fm-forge-detect.sh on the real SlnkFindMy clone proposes forge=gerrit with its evidence; a GitHub clone proposes none; a non-git directory exits 2 | ✅ pass | live | live-intake.log S1 |

   A failure prints a typed error record instead; fix what it names and publish again, which updates the same change rather than creating another.
Then append `done [at=<epoch>]: PR {change url} published for review` to the status file and stop. You are finished.
That `done:` is accepted only when the change's current patch set on the server carries this copy's HEAD tree, so commit nothing after publishing; if you must change the work, commit it and publish again before reporting done.
There is no pull request, no `gh-axi` call, and no forge CI result to report: a human reviewer approves and submits the change on the server, and firstmate relays that outcome.

title: feat(bin): land the verified jcode crewmate and scout adapter
body:
## What this lands

The verified jcode crewmate/scout adapter, which was written and verified earlier
but never pushed anywhere. Without it, a firstmate session running from the
default branch has no jcode support at all: `bin/fm-harness.sh` and
`bin/fm-spawn.sh` contain zero references to jcode. On 2026-09-23 that cost a
working day - Claude launches were refused by a consent record on one project
and the Pi fallback by third-party billing, leaving jcode the only usable
runtime on the machine and firstmate unable to reach it.

### The adapter commits

Three of the four original commits are rebased here unchanged:

- `feat(bin): add verified jcode crewmate adapter`
- `feat(bin): verify jcode as a primary supervision harness`
- `fix(bin): recognise jcode in session-lock harness identity`

The fourth original commit (`5f8c0e9d`, linked-worktree path in the same-branch
run inventory reader) is **deliberately absent**. The default branch already
fixes that same failure a better way, reading the repository path from the
overview's own `repo:` line instead of guessing between candidate paths
(`bin/fm-nm-run-lib.sh`). Carrying the older fix would have reintroduced the
guess. The required behaviour is present without it.

## Two corrections included, and why

Both were commissioned for this change from failures observed on 2026-09-23.
They are separate commits and deliberately small. Landing the adapter with
either hole open would ship a runtime firstmate cannot reliably control, which
is the opposite of the point.

**1. jcode's numbered composer could not be read, so its agents could not be
stopped.** jcode numbers its composer prompt (`1>`, `2>`, `1<>` once submitted)
instead of drawing a prompt glyph, and draws a context meter and status glyph at
the row's far right. A bare `>` is a shell prompt, which the classifier must
refuse, so every jcode pane classified `unknown` at every width from 40 to 200
columns, empty or typed alike. That is not cosmetic: `bin/fm-control.sh` refuses
to type an exit command unless the composer is proven empty, and
`fm-spawn.sh --relaunch` then refuses because the endpoint still reads alive. Two
stalled workers were recoverable only by terminating the agent processes
directly.

The row is now normalized before classification, and only for a pane whose
foreground process is structurally identified as jcode, mirroring the existing
Cursor process-identity gate. The shared resolvers are untouched, so no other
harness's dead-shell rule is weakened. The leading digits are what make this
safe: a dead shell prompt is `>`, `$`, `%`, or `#` alone and never `1>`, so a
numbered prompt is positive proof of jcode's composer, while a bare prompt on a
jcode pane still reads `unknown` and still refuses the lifecycle action.

Verified live on jcode v0.86.0 and v0.87.1: empty reads empty, typed reads
pending, at 40, 60 and 200 columns, and a real jcode agent now accepts the
guarded exit and stops cleanly. jcode joins the live composer-matrix guard.

**2. A cold jcode daemon refused legitimate spawns.** The preflight refused on a
single unanswered `jcode debug sessions`, but the daemon starts lazily and loses
that first query while binding its debug socket. Observed: a refused spawn
followed seconds later by the identical command reporting ok with no
intervention. The query is now retried over a bounded window
(`FM_JCODE_DEBUG_WAIT`, default 10s). A daemon that is genuinely down still
fails, after every attempt in the window has missed, so this widens the evidence
rather than weakening the check, and the bound keeps a wedged daemon from
stalling a spawn.

## The preflight is split by what it can know without a daemon

Do not re-order this. Review during this change moved the whole preflight to run
*before* the pane launch, on the reasoning that a bad jcode home must never reach
a pane. That was reverted, because the preflight's live daemon probe cannot pass
before a launch: only a launch brings the daemon up. Reproduced directly by
pointing the client at a socket with no daemon behind it, the debug command fails
and starts nothing:

```
Debug socket not found at ".../jcode-...-debug.sock"
Make sure:
  1. A jcode server is running (jcode or jcode serve)
```

In that ordering the first jcode spawn after a reboot would be refused forever -
precisely the situation this change exists to fix, and a worse failure than the
cold-start flake the retry was added to smooth.

The preflight is therefore split:

- **Before the launch**, `--static` runs only the checks that answer from
  configuration alone: onboarding complete, provider connected,
  `display.debug_socket` configured, and the firstmate-owns-dispatch checks
  (swarm off, `swarm`/`schedule`/`initiative` denied, ambient off). All four were
  confirmed to pass with no daemon running, so the never-reach-a-pane goal is
  fully served here.
- **After the launch**, the live daemon probe runs where it originally did, with
  its bounded retry.

The earlier end-to-end test could not catch the regression, because its fake
jcode always answered. A cold case now drives the real `bin/fm-spawn.sh` with no
daemon answering until the launch command runs, and asserts the spawn still
succeeds. Moving the probe back before the launch makes that test fail with the
exact refusal above, so it fails for the right reason.

## jcode's role boundary

jcode is verified as a primary and for crewmate and scout work, and is refused
as a secondmate. `AGENTS.md`, the harness-adapters skill, and the jcode harness
reference all record that consistently, and `bin/fm-spawn.sh` refuses a
secondmate launch so the boundary cannot be bypassed by a raw harness argument.

## CI

This repository's CI may be affected by an account-level GitHub Actions billing
failure unrelated to this change. Check state is reported as observed rather
than assumed.

title: fix(bin): read Kimi 2.0.2's composer and close the endpoint when a Kimi launch gate fails
body:
## Objective

A Kimi 2.0.2 crewmate launched on the Herdr backend was recorded as a FAILED spawn while the agent had in fact started and was working — leaving a real worker running with no task record and no supervision. That is worse than a failed launch: nothing watches it, nothing can steer it, and teardown does not know it exists.

## Cause

Two independent faults, both fixed here.

1. **Composer misread.** Kimi 2.0.2 renders a mode row and a context row *below* its bordered input box. The shared screen classifier did not recognise those rows as furniture, so `fm_backend_herdr_composer_state` never returned a confident verdict and `fm-spawn`'s readiness wait timed out. Under tmux the same launch reads correctly, which is why this presents as Herdr-only.

2. **Leaked endpoint on a gate failure.** When the Kimi launch gate failed, `fm-spawn` recorded the failure but did not close the endpoint it had already launched. The agent kept running, unrecorded.

## What changed

- `bin/fm-composer-lib.sh` treats Kimi's mode and context rows as furniture when they sit below a *proven bordered box*. The match is deliberately narrow: a foreign row in that position still refuses, so an unidentified pane is never mistaken for an empty composer.
- `bin/fm-spawn.sh` routes Kimi gate failures through the shared `spawn_gate_endpoint_cleanup`, so an unconfirmed brief delivery can no longer leave a running unrecorded worker.
- `tests/fm-composer-lib.test.sh` gains portable regressions for the widened footer rules, including nonzero-usage rows, narrow panes, and a spaced default-model name at max effort.
- Verification record added to `docs/verification/runtime-backends.md`; the Kimi harness reference records the 2.0.2 behaviour.

## Verification

Verified live against a real Kimi 2.0.2 session in an isolated Herdr lab, not against fixtures:

- before/after `fm_backend_herdr_composer_state`: `unknown` -> `empty` when idle, `unknown` -> `pending` when text is typed.
- `tests/fm-composer-lib.test.sh` 36 ok; `fm-backend-herdr` 207 ok; the kimi-harness, composer-ghost and spawn suites and lint all green.

## Why the second fix matters most

The composer misread wastes a launch. The leaked endpoint loses a worker: it keeps consuming quota, keeps editing a worktree, and no supervisor knows to look at it. A launch that fails loudly is recoverable; a launch that fails while succeeding is not.

## Risk

LOW. The classifier change is additive and narrowed to a proven bordered box. The spawn change closes an endpoint on a path that already treated the launch as failed.

title: fix(calm): make the Pi sprite link portable across broken symlink checkouts
body:
.pi/extensions/lib/fm-calm-working-ship-sprite.ts was a tracked git symlink
(mode 120000) into .claude/mods/firstmate-calm/lib/fm-calm-working-ship-sprite.ts.
On a filesystem/git configuration that does not materialize real symlinks
(confirmed on a Windows checkout with core.symlinks effectively disabled), the
working tree gets a plain text file containing only the literal target path
string, and .pi/extensions/fm-calm.ts then fails to parse it as TypeScript,
breaking Pi extension loading (and the no-mistakes review step) for every
task in the repo on that machine.

Replace the tracked symlink with a plain, real TypeScript file (git mode
100644) that re-exports everything from the canonical sprite core via a
normal relative import. This needs no filesystem symlink support at all, so
it resolves identically everywhere pi -e runs, while keeping the canonical
sprite geometry, bounce track, cadences, and freeze/resume state living in
exactly one place (required by Claude Code's own hooks-module loader, which
refuses to import a file from outside its plugin folder).

tests/fm-calm-claude-mod.test.sh's test_plugin_shape previously asserted the
Pi path was an OS symlink resolving to the same file; that assertion cannot
hold for a plain re-export, so it now imports both modules and checks
identical export sets plus function reference identity, which still fails a
future regression to a duplicated (drifting) copy.

tests/fm-calm-pi-extension.test.sh's fixtures cp the tracked sprite file into
several isolated, flattened directories that do not mirror the real repo
tree; a relative-import re-export cannot resolve there, so WORKING_SHIP_SPRITE
now points directly at the mod's self-contained canonical file instead of the
Pi-side re-export shim, giving those fixtures the same complete, dependency-free
copy a dereferenced symlink used to produce.

The repo's other two tracked symlinks (.agents/skills/firstmate-calm and
.claude/skills, both directory symlinks used only for Claude Code's own
plugin/skill discovery, never imported as executable code) exhibit the same
underlying checkout defect on the affected machine: they also materialize as
plain text files there. Unlike the sprite file, nothing in the running
product imports them as code, so the practical effect is silent
(Claude Code simply would not discover the mod on that checkout) rather than
a parse crash - except that tests/fm-calm-claude-mod.test.sh's own -L
assertion on .agents/skills/firstmate-calm already fails hard in that
environment, independent of this change (reproduced against origin/main
HEAD before any local edits). Left as-is: both are long-standing,
intentional, documented conventions (AGENTS.md), fixing them would mean
restructuring those conventions or the directory-symlink model entirely, and
CI never runs this suite on a checkout with broken symlink materialization
(ubuntu-latest and macos-latest both materialize real symlinks).

title: fix(bin): stop the repeating watcher recovery wake, and stop reading a busy watcher as hung
body:
Two faults in the same area left a 38-task home with no live watcher for stretches of hours, while costing a supervision turn every few minutes.

**The recovery wake repeated forever.** When a watcher start found an announced but unacknowledged downtime episode, it minted a fresh generation, which invalidated the acknowledgement command the handling turn had already been given. That acknowledgement then reported a newer episode and asked for a re-drain, and the next turn boundary invalidated the new one the same way. Every turn announced recovery, exited on that wake, and left nothing supervising in between. The reopen now keeps the episode's own generation, so the outstanding acknowledgement lands.

The acknowledgement also now retires an episode whose presented rows it consumed, even when a row appended during handling is still queued. Previously a busy home could never empty the queue at that moment, so no acknowledgement could settle the episode. That row still resurfaces through its own wake or the next start's recovery check.

**A healthy watcher read as wedged.** The liveness beacon was touched once per cycle, but a cycle's work scales with the fleet: a check sweep spends up to `FM_CHECK_TIMEOUT` per registered check, and the pane scan captures every recorded window, so cycles ran 300-1000s against a 300s grace. Every later arm then refused to attach to a live pid with a stale beacon, started a second watcher that could only exit, and the guard reported supervision as hung. The watcher now beats at each proven-progress point inside a cycle, so beacon age bounds progress rather than cycle turnover.

Sampling a live "hung" watcher showed it forking and reading subshells continuously - read 1377, wait4 247, fork 42 of 1754 samples. It was working, not parked.

Measured on a home with 36-38 task records, where both shapes reproduced.

title: Reclaim unowned /tmp lane scratch daily and at teardown
body:
## Summary

Lane scratch under `/tmp` had no owner after a task ended. Pool teardown returns the slot and removes the recorded `tasktmp=` directory, and nothing removed `/tmp/hhe*`, `/tmp/jest_rs`, or Claude session directories.

`bin/fm-tmp-sweep.sh` is that owner.

- Teardown removes names that are exactly the task id, or that id followed by `-`, `.`, `_`, or `+`, when no live process working directory remains under them. A short or non-path-safe id removes nothing.
- The watcher runs the aged sweep at most once a day. It removes `/tmp/hhe*` entries, the exact directory `/tmp/jest_rs`, and `/tmp/claude-1000/<project>/<session>` once they are older than three days, still only with no live process working directory under them. A live task record keeps its own `hhe` issue prefix.
- The recorded `/tmp/fm-<task>/` root stays on teardown's existing removal.

Docker images, the OpenCode store, and native Muse sessions are not removed by this change. A dry-run report for this host lists those as separate decisions, including a few mail and pdf files under `/tmp/hhe*` that the age gate would remove.

## Test

`bash tests/fm-tmp-sweep.test.sh`

The cases use a fixture directory and an injected working-directory list. They do not touch the host `/tmp`.

title: fix(bin): run the session lock, herdr spawns, and claim locks on native Windows
body:
## Intent

Make firstmate run on native Windows (Git Bash / MSYS) with Claude Code inside herdr, then send the fixes upstream as a PR. On this host every session opened read-only because the session-lock harness ancestry walk could not see the native claude.exe process (MSYS ps ignores -o and reports native parents as PID 0/1); this is upstream issues #3396, #3653, #1508. Decision: keep one process-identity primitive in bin/fm-session-lock-lib.sh that reads Win32_Process via one PowerShell Get-CimInstance call when /proc/<pid>/winpid exists, and keep every recorded pid in the Windows pid namespace that Claude Code already uses for CLAUDE_PID, so liveness checks on the recorded lock pid work (a gap in the competing PR #4616, whose liveness check still used kill -0 and ps). The MSYS part of the chain is climbed through /proc first because a fork child's Win32 ParentProcessId can be transient. POSIX hosts must behave exactly as before. Second fix: native Windows herdr reports C:\...\herdr.sock socket paths, which fm_backend_herdr_canonical_socket_path refused, so every herdr spawn failed its launcher-identity proof (issue #3283); drive-letter paths are converted with cygpath first and refused when cygpath is absent. Third fix, found while verifying: Git Bash ln -s deep-copies directories by default, so the symlink claim lock in bin/fm-wake-lib.sh could never be reclaimed from a dead holder and nested .steal directories until session start hit its 120 s bound; fm_lock_symlink requests native Windows symlinks (winsymlinks:nativestrict, which fails instead of copying when Windows refuses, i.e. without Developer Mode), and the owner comparison accepts both MSYS spellings of one Windows path because readlink reports Temp paths as /tmp. Verified live on Windows 11: bin/fm-lock.sh acquires the lock for claude.exe and bin/fm-session-start.sh completes without the read-only banner. Some existing tests (a symlinked-sidecar case, the e2e lock tests, fm-watcher-lock) fail on Windows both before and after this change because they depend on POSIX ps/symlink semantics; making those suites Windows-portable is out of scope.

## What Changed

- **Session lock (`bin/fm-session-lock-lib.sh`):** On native Windows (Git Bash / MSYS, detected when `/proc/<pid>/winpid` exists), the harness ancestry walk now climbs the MSYS part of the chain through `/proc`. From the topmost process's winpid it continues through `Win32_Process` rows, read with one `Get-CimInstance` call, so it can find the native `claude.exe` ancestor instead of opening the session read-only. Recorded pids stay in the Windows pid namespace, and liveness checks go through the same process-identity primitive instead of `kill -0`/`ps`. POSIX hosts use the same code paths as before.
- **herdr backend (`bin/backends/herdr.sh`):** `fm_backend_herdr_canonical_socket_path` now converts drive-letter socket paths (`C:\...\herdr.sock`) to their POSIX spelling with `cygpath -u` and refuses them when `cygpath` is missing. Before this, every native-Windows herdr spawn failed its launcher-identity proof.
- **Claim locks (`bin/fm-wake-lib.sh`):** A new `fm_lock_symlink` publishes lock links with `winsymlinks:nativestrict` on MINGW/MSYS/Cygwin. Git Bash's default `ln -s` deep-copies directories, so the old code never produced a real symlink. With `nativestrict`, `ln -s` fails outright instead of copying. `fm_lock_points_to_owner` now also accepts both MSYS spellings of one Windows path (for example, `/tmp` vs the Temp path) by comparing their `cygpath -w` forms, and the stray-owner-link cleanup uses the same check. The result: a lock held by a dead holder can be reclaimed again, where before each reclaim attempt nested another `.steal` directory. New `tests/fm-lock-reclaim.test.sh` (registered in `fm-test-run.sh`) plus new cases in the herdr backend and session-lock ancestry tests cover these paths.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Risk Assessment

✅ Low: Both round-1 fixes check out against the current code. The stray-link cleanup now uses fm_lock_points_to_owner, so both MSYS spellings of a path match. On POSIX, the kill -0 check again runs only in fm_harness_pid_alive, and the trusted-id and inspect paths once more read identity through ps alone. Windows-only behavior sits behind the /proc winpid and uname checks, and tests run it through the real public functions.

## Testing

I drove every intent scenario live on the Windows 11 / Git Bash host inside Claude Code and compared each against the base commit. fm-lock.sh acquires, reports held, and re-acquires for claude.exe, while the base fails with "cannot locate harness process in ancestry". A dead Windows pid or a live non-harness pid is reclaimed. Another live claude.exe holding the lock is refused. The claim lock is a native Windows symlink: it is reclaimed from a dead holder, it refuses a contender with no stray link left behind, and release leaves nothing. The base deep-copies the directory, cannot reclaim, and leaves .steal directories. In a guarded fm-lab Herdr session, the launcher-identity proof accepts herdr's C:\ socket, while the base refuses it, and with no cygpath on PATH the path is still refused. fm-session-start.sh completes with the lock held and no read-only banner, while the base prints the banner. The POSIX scenario was not driven live: WSL Linux test-suite runs pass except one pty-host reparent e2e test, which fails the same way on base, but that is test coverage, not a live product session. The Windows-side failures I saw are also pre-existing (the symlinked-sidecar case matches the intent's out-of-scope list; the Herdr stale-shadowing-client test also fails on base). The Herdr lab was torn down, the default session was never touched, no processes were left behind, and the worktree is clean. The temp scratch dir under OS Temp could not be removed because a security policy blocks recursive rm.

When this session owns supervision and away mode is not active:
1. Drain first with `bin/fm-wake-drain.sh`.
   After handling all emitted wakes and reconciling open decisions and unread status lines, run the exact `--ack-through` command printed as `WAKE_ACK_REQUIRED`; until then the work remains durable for idempotent re-handling after interruption.
2. Routine watcher arm and re-arm are owned by the Stop `asyncRewake` hook (`bin/fm-claude-stop-autoarm.sh`), never by you.
   Every turn end while supervision is needed launches or attaches one home-scoped watcher cycle with no model command and no model tokens.
   An actionable close wakes you through the hook's exit-2 rewake, delivered as a `Stop hook feedback` message.
3. On a `Stop hook feedback` wake (`signal:`, `stale:`, `check:`, or `heartbeat`), run `bin/fm-wake-drain.sh` first and handle the wake.
   Do not run `bin/fm-watch-arm.sh` after an ordinary wake; the next turn end re-arms automatically when supervision is still needed.
   Do not invent a wake from an attach-status line alone; drain and act only on real wake records, the drain's `OPEN DECISIONS` and `UNREAD STATUS` entries, or a real watcher reason line.
4. On the one `Stop hook feedback` automatic-mechanism failure notice (`firstmate watcher auto-arm FAILED ...`), drain, inspect the automatic mechanism failure, and do not turn the notice into a repeating manual-arm loop.
5. If the Stop hook does not claim the home or reports an exhausted failure, inspect its registration and watcher startup path before ending blind.
   Keep the Stop-owned automatic mechanism as the only Claude arm owner.
6. Treat `watcher: started ...` and `watcher: attached ...` inside automatic arm output as proof that one live cycle exists.
   On attach, the arm follows verified identity-matched successors instead of exiting when the first cycle ends.
7. The durable wake queue preserves actionable events between a rewake and the next Stop-launched arm, while the bounded turn-end guard prevents a blind Stop when recovery did not start.
   No PreToolUse hook denies fleet commands based on watcher status.
   [`watcher-continuity.md`](../watcher-continuity.md) owns the exact session-lock recovery boundary.
8. The turn-end guard (`bin/fm-turnend-guard.sh --claude`) remains the final backstop.
   It requires the PID-strict live-watcher and fresh-beacon predicate at the Stop boundary, except for the Claude-specific foreign-live-owner safe exit owned by [`turnend-guard.md`](../turnend-guard.md#guard-predicates); that document also owns the distinct model-aware mid-turn pull-guard rules.
   Otherwise, it allows the stop when a watcher is healthy or an open auto-arm generation claim owns recovery, while fresh failure epochs advance the bounded one-time attended fail-open progression described there.
9. Waiting on the hook-owned cycle is silent: do not send idle progress while the watcher is parked.

The watcher itself remains `bin/fm-watch.sh`, and `bin/fm-watch-arm.sh` remains the verified arm wrapper that the Stop hook foregrounds.
Re-arm attaches to an existing healthy cycle when one is already present and follows its verified successor chain.
See [`watcher-continuity.md`](../watcher-continuity.md) for the arm-layer successor and clean-close failure contract and the Claude ownership model.


================================================================================
READ-ONCE CONTRACT
================================================================================
Everything below is printed in full for this session start: every state/*.meta,
a compact data/backlog.md listing, a bounded tail of every state/*.status,
data/projects.md, data/secondmates.md, data/captain.md, data/captain-shared.md,
and data/learnings.md.
Do NOT re-read any of them after reading this digest, and do NOT bulk-read
data/backlog.md or state/*.status: re-reading everything defeats the entire
point of this command.

Go to a source directly only when:
  - this digest flagged it ABSENT (then rebuild or create it per AGENTS.md),
  - its contents looked unparseable or corrupt,
  - an individual full status log is needed for older wake-event history, or a
    status line was capped and its tail matters (each task's full log path is
    printed with its tail),
  - a full task body is needed (bin/fm-tasks-axi.sh show <id> --full, or data/backlog.md),
  - the backlog listing disclosed omitted queued items and this turn needs them,

<summary>🔧 **Review** - 2 issues found → auto-fixed ✅</summary>

- ⚠️ `bin/fm-wake-lib.sh:519` - fm_lock_remove_stray_owner_link still compares readlink output to $ownerdir with a raw string `=`. That misses the rule this change added to fm_lock_points_to_owner, which says both MSYS spellings of one Windows path must compare equal. How it fails: on Git Bash with native symlinks, a contended fm_lock_try_create runs `ln -s ownerdir lockdir` while lockdir is a live symlink to the holder's owner dir. ln then creates lockdir/<basename> inside the holder's owner dir, and fm_lock_symlink's non-zero exit sends control to fm_lock_remove_stray_owner_link. When STATE is under Windows Temp, readlink gives /tmp/... while ownerdir is /c/Users/.../Temp/..., so the stray link is never removed. The holder's later rmdir of its owner dir then fails because the dir is not empty, and each contended attempt leaks one more entry. Fix: call `fm_lock_points_to_owner "$stray" "$ownerdir"` instead of the raw comparison. That is the only remaining raw readlink comparison against an owner path in the file. The other readlink consumers (lines 489, 610, 1026, 1077, 1159) either compare a spelling with itself or already go through fm_lock_points_to_owner.
- ℹ️ `bin/fm-session-lock-lib.sh:331` - The intent says "POSIX hosts must behave exactly as before", but on POSIX fm_session_lock_trusted_session_id now runs through _fm_proc_identity. That adds a `kill -0` check the old code did not have: it read identity with `ps` alone. If kill -0 fails with EPERM (CLAUDE_PID is owned by another uid, e.g. the harness runs as root and the shell drops privileges), the trusted session id is no longer returned where it used to be. The sequence is rare, but it is a POSIX behavior change. Smallest fix: keep the `kill -0` gate in fm_harness_pid_alive's POSIX branch only, and let _fm_proc_identity's POSIX branch use ps alone, as the old trusted-id path did. fm_session_lock_inspect's result is unchanged either way, because _fm_proc_exists keeps the ps fallback.

🔧 Fix applied.
